vectors.enisa_quote: overtaking control of the management segment to execute malicious commands
vectors.reason: Control of the management (TT&C ground) segment is taken and used to issue commands.

vectors.enisa_quote: adversaries taking control of space assets
vectors.reason: ENISA gives no access path for the takeover; the rogue ground station origin is included by the project lead's decision.

rows.reason: Suppressing FDIR, watchdogs and limit checks so actions go unnoticed is a way to stop the satellite doing its service, while ENISA's seizure text only speaks of commands and user lockout.
Making ground software render or interpret telemetry wrongly hides the spacecraft's true state from controllers, an operator-blinding step the seizure text never mentions.
Pausing telemetry publishers or filtering packets on board to leave controllers uninformed is concealment, and ENISA says nothing about hiding the takeover.
Falsifying counters, flags and reporting modes that operators judge command hygiene by is a cover-up tactic that the ENISA takeover sentence does not describe.
Turning command receivers off to create quiet windows closes the command path, whereas ENISA's attacker wants to use the command path to issue commands.
Biasing the receiver AGC so that specific commands are not processed defeats reception of commands, and ENISA describes commands being executed, not suppressed.
Reading or faking command-lock and frame-lock indicators to test geometry or readiness is link reconnaissance that ENISA's text on taking control does not mention.
Switching telemetry downlink modes or virtual-channel selections to change what ground sees is reporting manipulation, which ENISA does not tie to seizure.
Toggling cryptographic modes or 'crypto off' selectors to desynchronise ground and spacecraft is a mode change, whereas ENISA names overtaking access control without describing mode selectors.
Biasing the spacecraft clock so logs and command histories look shifted is a time-evasion trick, and ENISA names no time manipulation.
Extending or disabling watchdog timeouts to let long processes run unreset is a stealth tweak that the seizure description does not include.
Abusing relaxed rate, size and timetag checks during safe-mode is a timing trick tied to a vehicle state, which the ENISA text does not mention.
Editing the on-board whitelist to run or hide malicious programs presumes an implanted program, while ENISA names exploited vulnerabilities and commands.
A rootkit patches flight-software APIs and telemetry publishers to hide an implant, and ENISA describes no implant that needs hiding.
A bootkit runs first in the boot chain to shape what later layers see, which presupposes a planted boot component that the seizure text does not describe.
Dazzling or spoofing the spacecraft's own proximity sensors targets space-situational awareness, not the command or access-control path ENISA says is seized.
Corrupting ground-based space-domain-awareness catalogues and sensor networks blinds monitoring, which has no link to taking control of a satellite.
Using valid credentials in a way that conceals the intruder is an evasion behaviour, and ENISA names no concealment.
Two or more compromised modules cooperating to hide activity assumes supply-chain implants, which ENISA's seizure sentence does not describe.
Executing an implant only when orbital geometry or lighting conditions match is a trigger condition, and ENISA gives no trigger or implant.

rows.sparta_quote: The adversary alters how the spacecraft validates authority
rows.reason: Altering how the spacecraft validates authority is how access control is overtaken.
Manipulating boot ROM vectors and loaders so attacker code runs before integrity checks is a firmware-level foothold, not the access-control or command takeover ENISA names.
Exploiting errata, scan chains and debug straps in the hardware design is one narrow flaw class, whereas ENISA says only 'existing vulnerabilities' without hardware detail.
Issuing low-level maintenance or register-write device commands that bypass command mediation is a hardware-level abuse, not the exploitation of existing vulnerabilities ENISA describes.
Putting links or storage into clear or weakened protection by toggling flags or forcing null ciphers is the SLE/SDL compromise of ENISA's hijacking threat, not this seizure text.
Keying execution to a fixed wall-clock epoch describes a time-triggered implant, and ENISA names no triggered code.

rows.sparta_quote: abusing defects in software that runs on the vehicle
rows.reason: ENISA says control of space assets is taken by exploiting existing vulnerabilities.
Flight-software parsers, table loaders and safing logic are one subclass of code flaws, and ENISA's 'existing vulnerabilities' does not name flight software specifically.
Kernel and scheduler flaws in Linux-style spacecraft operating systems are a further narrowing of code flaws that the ENISA wording does not make.
Introducing native binaries, shellcode or interpreted data payloads is injection of malicious code, while ENISA's seizure text names exploited vulnerabilities rather than injected code.
A rootkit that interposes on state-reporting mechanisms hides other implants, which is the malware-injection scenario rather than a takeover through vulnerabilities.
A bootkit placed in the pre-OS boot chain is an injected implant, a different scenario from the vulnerability exploitation and access-control takeover in ENISA's text.
Timing on-board actions for safe-mode, when guardrails change, depends on a vehicle state that the ENISA text does not mention.
Altering live registers, limit tables and schedule data is the parameter-modification scenario, not the command seizure and access-control lockout ENISA describes here.
Writing internal registers while flight software runs changes subsystem behaviour, and ENISA names no register tampering.
Rewriting message-ID to subscriber routing maps redirects on-board data flow, which ENISA does not mention for seizure of control.
Editing app or subscriber tables changes which software receives which message class, a table-level edit that ENISA does not enumerate.
Skewing scheduler parameters and timer tables to alter task timing is a parameter-modification effect, not part of seizing control through commands.
Editing thruster calibration, valve timing and delta-V tables is a propulsion-specific change, whereas ENISA's takeover sentence names no subsystem.
Altering star-tracker catalogues, gyro biases and controller gains is an attitude-control manipulation that ENISA's text does not mention.
Changing bus voltage limits and MPPT setpoints concerns the power subsystem, which the seizure text leaves out.
Editing opcode-to-handler maps and queue limits in command and data handling is a C&DH table change that ENISA does not describe as the means of takeover.
Changing watchdog timeouts, reset actions and enable masks is a parameter edit of the watchdog, not one of the takeover steps in ENISA's description.
Writing clock registers or time-distribution settings alters the time base, and ENISA mentions no timing change.
Overwhelming a link or processing path with traffic is a denial-of-service action, while ENISA's seizure threat is a takeover that needs the commands to be accepted.
Saturating the spacecraft with valid telecommands or no-ops so it burns resources honouring them is flooding, the opposite of the targeted malicious commands ENISA describes.
Injecting noise or malformed frames that receivers waste effort rejecting is jamming-like input, and ENISA's attacker needs commands to be accepted.
Forging time tags, sensor measurements or bus messages so on-board logic acts on false inputs is spoofing, not the exploitation of existing vulnerabilities and access control ENISA names.
Forging or biasing the time that on-board consumers see to break timetag validation is a time-input attack, and ENISA names no time manipulation.
Forging frames on 1553, SpaceWire or CAN buses requires bus access and is not the vulnerability or access-control takeover that ENISA describes.
Presenting fabricated sensor measurements as ground truth is data deception, not the command seizure and lockout ENISA states.
Transmitting GNSS-like signals to steer the navigation solution is a navigation-spoofing attack that ENISA does not link to seizure of control.
Learning secrets from power, timing or emissions side channels is data exfiltration, and ENISA states an availability loss, not data theft.
Capturing electromagnetic leakage from switching chips to infer computation is a proximity exfiltration route and ENISA states no exfiltration.
Timing acknowledgments and response latencies to learn which code path ran is a side-channel measurement that has no role in the described takeover.
Co-opting a backup rekey or beacon link as a covert data path is exfiltration, which ENISA's seizure text does not describe.
Retuning carriers or adding subcarriers so mission data leaves over an unmonitored path is exfiltration by radio reconfiguration, with no basis in ENISA's text.
Adding a subcarrier or new waveform to an SDR to piggyback payload data is covert exfiltration and ENISA names no data leaving the system.
Remapping transponder paths or frequencies to route traffic to non-mission receivers is a communications-configuration exfiltration, not command seizure.
Siphoning mission data at scale from a compromised ground system is a data-breach scenario, while ENISA's seizure text states no data theft.
Breaching a developer or integration site for source code and build artefacts is a third-party supply-chain route, not the exploitation of existing vulnerabilities in ENISA's text.
Capturing mission data at commercial ground stations or relay partners is partner-site data theft, and ENISA's seizure sentence includes no data theft.
Routing stolen data over a payload's own downlink after implanting code in the payload follows a malicious-code implant that ENISA's seizure text does not describe.
Inserting malicious code or configuration during manufacturing and delivery is the supply-chain threat, whereas ENISA's takeover occurs in operations by exploiting existing vulnerabilities.
Poisoned dependencies, container images and IDE plugins compromise the build toolchain, which is a supply-chain action and not what the seizure text says.
Swapping signed binaries, subverting update metadata or using stolen signing keys targets delivered software, which ENISA does not name for seizure.
Hardware Trojans in ASIC/FPGA designs or tampered boards are inserted before delivery, which ENISA's operational takeover does not describe.
A compromised software-defined radio gives a foothold through reconfigurable waveforms and bitstreams, and ENISA names no radio or payload-radio compromise.
Pivoting from a compromised neighbour over an inter-satellite link is a crosslink origin that ENISA's text on the management segment does not mention.
Using a secondary or backup communication channel with different monitoring is a door ENISA does not name; it speaks of the management segment.
Establishing presence on a standby MOC or alternate commercial station concerns the backup ground path, not the primary management segment of ENISA's takeover.
Using a spacecraft's backup RF receive path needs that cross-strapped receiver, which ENISA's seizure text does not name.
Co-orbiting and approaching the target for local sensing or contact is a proximity approach, and ENISA gives no physical or on-orbit access path.
Analysing unintentional emissions from nearby to infer keys and counters is a proximity eavesdropping step that ENISA does not describe.
Exploiting docking, berthing or servicing capture as a high-trust bridge between vehicles requires an OSAM contact that ENISA's text does not mention.
Grappling a target with a robotic arm or coupler to touch covers and umbilicals is physical proximity access, which is absent from ENISA's description.
Entering through a hosted payload's own command and file services is an alternate door into the host that ENISA's seizure text does not name.

rows.sparta_quote: manipulate authentication material and counters to pass checks
rows.reason: Compromising the ground segment gives the access to manipulate authentication material, which leads to the overtaking of access control.
Manipulating the pipeline that builds and uplinks on-orbit updates delivers altered software, whereas ENISA describes malicious commands and exploited vulnerabilities, not a pushed update.

rows.sparta_quote: transmit legitimate-looking commands to the target spacecraft
rows.reason: Sending commands through the seized management segment is the way the malicious commands reach the spacecraft.

rows.sparta_quote: Most interact by radiating or exchanging traffic using mission-compatible waveforms, framing, or crosslink protocols
rows.reason: An external transmitter sending mission-compatible signals reaches the vulnerable on-board code and the validation of authority through the radio link.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries may field their own ground system, transportable or fixed, to transmit and receive mission-compatible signals
rows.reason: A rogue ground station delivers the exploit, the access-control change and the malicious commands over the radio link.
A rogue satellite phasing into a nearby orbit to act as a local RF peer requires a space-based attacker that ENISA does not describe; the lead chose only the rogue ground station.
Counterspace weapons that jam or spoof links or directly impose effects belong to the anti-satellite threat, while ENISA's seizure text describes taking control by commands.
Riding trusted partner, vendor and user-community connections is an alternative first-execution route, and ENISA's text does not describe a trust relationship.
Compromising a university instrument builder or international collaborator through shared portals is a collaboration route that ENISA does not name.
A vendor with persistent administrative access to ground software and modems is a third-party supplier route, not the seizure ENISA describes.
Entering through customer terminals, gateways and tasking portals uses the user segment as a door, which ENISA's wording about the management segment excludes.
Timing first execution to safe-mode, when contingency command sets are enabled, ties the entry to a vehicle state that ENISA does not mention.
Abusing removable media or peripherals ingested during integration or operations is an auxiliary-device door that ENISA's seizure text does not describe.
Compromising test controllers, EGSE and loaders during assembly and launch operations happens before flight, while ENISA's takeover concerns the operational management segment.
Reaching a hosted payload through the host spacecraft bus is an inverse hosted-payload door, and ENISA names no hosted payload.
Triggering an existing spacecraft function for a harmful purpose is a different outcome from the malicious commands and user lockout that ENISA states.
Forcing or blocking a mode or state transition is an effect that ENISA does not state; it names commands being executed and users being locked out.

SPARTA limits Configuration Manipulation to non-executable settings and excludes executable changes, and the key replacement behind the lockout is carried by PER-0004, so ENISA's lockout sentence is not described by this row separately.
Falsifying sensor, stored or processed information is the data-modification scenario, and ENISA states no altered data.
Injecting unauthorized commands is the outcome ENISA states.
Replacing firmware or loading altered programmable logic changes the implementation itself, which ENISA's command-and-access-control takeover does not describe.
Depleting or monopolising a finite spacecraft resource such as power or bandwidth is exhaustion, which ENISA's seizure sentence does not claim.
Shifting the on-board clock or breaking synchronisation is a timing effect that ENISA's seizure text never mentions.
Pivoting across the host-payload boundary through SpaceWire or 1553 gateways is lateral movement, and ENISA describes no movement inside the spacecraft.
Forging message IDs on a flat bus with no segregation to influence other nodes is lateral spread that ENISA does not describe.
Hopping between constellation vehicles with crafted crosslink traffic needs a compromised first satellite and a constellation, which ENISA does not describe.
Escaping a separation-kernel or hypervisor partition through message ports or shared memory is an on-board pivot that ENISA's text lacks.
Crossing between rideshare payloads on shared launch infrastructure happens before separation, which ENISA's operational takeover does not cover.
Reusing operator accounts or station certificates to cross trust boundaries is abuse of granted rights, not the vulnerability exploitation and access-control takeover ENISA names.
Making malicious content survive resets by modifying boot ROM handoffs or non-volatile loaders is persistence of an implant, and ENISA names no implant.
A covert access path preinstalled by a supplier or inserted for re-entry is a backdoor scenario, not a takeover through existing vulnerabilities.
Hidden command handlers and alternate authentication checks inserted as code are an implanted backdoor, which ENISA's seizure text does not describe.
Residing long-term in operator workstations and schedulers is ground-side persistence, but ENISA states no lasting presence.

rows.role_reason: The lockout of legitimate users is the outcome ENISA states, so key replacement is coded as the impact rather than as persistence for its own sake.
rows.enisa_quote: complete lockout of legitimate satellite users by overtaking access control
rows.sparta_quote: so subsequent traffic must use the attacker’s keys to be accepted
rows.reason: Replacing the uplink keys makes legitimate users' traffic rejected, which is the lockout ENISA names.
Holding valid service or maintenance accounts to keep access is credential persistence, whereas ENISA's text describes overtaking access control without naming account use.
Compromising existing third-party or mission infrastructure to obtain ready-made reach is preparation that the kept chain does not need.
Compromising a mission's own ground system for preconfigured TT&C access is preparation that duplicates IA-0007, which the chain already keeps as the entry.
Acquiring uplink authentication and link-encryption keys beforehand is resource preparation that ENISA does not describe and the chain does not rely on.
Choosing between TT&C injection, payload downlinks or crosslinks as the delivery path is attack planning that the kept chain does not require.
Gathering RTOS versions and process layouts to find exploitable seams is reconnaissance that the kept chain does not need.
Collecting TT&C keys, counters and PN codes that would let the attacker authenticate is credential reconnaissance outside what ENISA describes.
Collecting architecture documents, SBOMs and toolchains to understand how flight software is built and signed is reconnaissance the chain does not need.
Enumerating IDEs, cross-compilers and container images used for flight builds is development-environment reconnaissance beyond the ENISA text.
Learning which analysers and fuzzers the programme uses to see what is untested is reconnaissance of test practice that ENISA does not describe.
Watching for sun-pointing and low-rate indicators that the spacecraft has entered safe-mode is reconnaissance for a safe-mode timing attack that ENISA does not describe.

notes: SDLS-on results assume an intact protocol: EX-0003 and EX-0009 act on code that has already accepted a command, so an outside transmitter without keys loses them when SDLS is on; the SDL protocol compromise itself is TR28.
